extracted.intended_audience: students, researchers, practitioners and members of the public interested in South African administrative law and the Promotion of Administrative Justice Act (PAJA)
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize and apply the PAJA standards for what counts as 'administrative action' and when such action must be procedurally fair, including related requirements for rulemaking, participation, training and oversight in South African administrative law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'administrative action' (s1, PAJA)
rubrics_metrics.description: PAJA defines 'administrative action' as any decision taken, or any failure to take a decision, by an organ of state (or a natural or juristic person exercising a public power or performing a public function in terms of an empowering provision) which adversely affects the rights of any person and which has a direct, external legal effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article reproduces PAJA's multi-part definition and emphasises that the statutory definition is 'considerably more complicated and qualified' than earlier drafts. It also summarises the test as: (a) a decision, (b) by an organ of state (or relevant person) exercising public power/function in terms of legislation/empowering provision, (c) that adversely affects rights, (d) that has direct, external legal effect, and (e) that is not specifically excluded by the Act's list of exclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision requirement (incl. failure to decide)
rubrics_metrics.description: An action will qualify only if it is a 'decision' (which includes a failure to take a decision); because 'decision' is confined to conduct 'of an administrative nature' in terms of an 'empowering provision', the definition must be read with 'empowering provision' and 'failure'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Currie & De Waal note the enquiry doesn't end with the definition of 'administrative action' – one must consider the definitions of 'decision', 'empowering provision' and 'failure' (the latter includes a refusal to take a decision). Practically, this means omissions/refusals can be administrative action if they meet the other elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empowering provision requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'decision' must be of an administrative nature made in terms of an 'empowering provision' (i.e., authority conferred by legislation or other empowering law).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because 'decision' is limited to acts under an empowering provision, a key inquiry is whether the power exercised originates in legislation or an equivalent empowering source; administrators must be acting under such authority for PAJA to apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adverse effect on rights and direct, external legal effect
rubrics_metrics.description: To be administrative action the decision must adversely affect the rights of any person and must have a direct, external legal effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article highlights these as conjunctive elements of the statutory test. Both factual/legal adverse impact and external legal consequence are required; minor internal actions without legal effect will typically fall outside PAJA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory exclusions to administrative action
rubrics_metrics.description: PAJA expressly excludes a list of matters from 'administrative action', including: (a) executive powers/functions of the National Executive, Provincial Executive or municipal council; (b) legislative functions of Parliament/provincial legislatures/municipal council; (c) judicial functions of judicial officers or certain tribunals; (d) decisions to institute or continue a prosecution; (e) decisions on appointment of judicial officers by the Judicial Service Commission; (f) decisions under the Promotion of Access to Information Act; and (g) decisions in terms of section 4(1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The detailed exclusions narrow PAJA's reach. The article reproduces the exclusion list and notes practitioners must check whether a challenged act falls into an excluded category before invoking PAJA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural fairness requirement (s3(1) & s3(2)(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 3(1): An administrative action which materially and adversely affects the rights or legitimate expectations of any person must be procedurally fair. Section 3(2)(a): A fair administrative procedure depends on the circumstances of each case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statutory rule is context-dependent: what procedural fairness demands will vary by situation. The article emphasises both the substantive trigger (material and adverse effect on rights/legitimate expectations) and the flexible, case-sensitive nature of the procedural fairness inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation emphasis: start with definition but read definitions together
rubrics_metrics.description: Although one begins with the definition of 'administrative action', the enquiry into the Act's scope does not end there; related statutory definitions must be read together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Currie & De Waal's commentary (quoted in the article) warns that legal analysis must link the definitions of 'administrative action', 'decision', 'empowering provision' and 'failure' rather than treating them in isolation when determining PAJA's application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public participation/notice-and-comment procedures are voluntary under PAJA
rubrics_metrics.description: PAJA introduced procedures to facilitate public participation (notice and comment, public inquiries), but these are essentially voluntary and it is unclear whether administrators will use them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes the provision for participatory procedures exists but was downgraded compared to earlier drafts; use is not mandated and uptake is uncertain. Practitioners should not assume mandatory notice-and-comment unless a specific provision or other law requires it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Code of good administrative conduct (s10(5A)/(6))
rubrics_metrics.description: PAJA provides for a code of good administrative conduct; a draft code has been produced and accessible but was not yet in force at the time described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The code is intended to guide administrators' behaviour; its draft status means its practical force may be limited until formally adopted. The article suggests the code's ultimate impact depends on promulgation and uptake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement (proposed) for administrators to publish/communicate rules – accessibility of rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Earlier Law Commission proposals required administrators to communicate their rules to those affected and to compile and maintain up-to-date registers and indexes of rules and standards; these requirements were dropped or watered down in the enacted PAJA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article criticises the omission, noting accessibility of rules is an express constitutional requirement and essential for the rule of law. Practically, administrators are encouraged (even if not strictly bound by PAJA) to make rules accessible and maintain indexes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scrutiny and control of delegated legislation – drafting protocols
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposals (partly rejected) would have required the State Law Adviser to compile and publish protocols for drafting rules/standards and provide training to drafters; an even stronger earlier proposal would have created a Central Drafting Office to scrutinise delegated legislation for clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article records that these measures were scaled back or dropped; the guidance implication is that better drafting controls and training are desirable to improve clarity and reduce maladministration, even where PAJA lacks mandatory mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Registers, national index and sunset provisions (periodic review of rules/standards)
rubrics_metrics.description: Earlier drafts proposed administrators compile registers and indexes and for an ARC to maintain a national index and consider 'sunset' automatic lapsing of rules; PAJA instead gives the Minister discretion to ask an advisory council about indexes, uniform rules, continuance of standards and automatic lapsing measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The enacted approach is cautious and largely discretionary. The article signals that periodic review and potential sunset clauses were seen as good practice but were not strongly implemented in PAJA; practitioners and reformers should press for regular review of delegated legislation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advisory council/Administrative Review Council (ARC) and non‑judicial review
rubrics_metrics.description: The Law Commission had proposed an ARC with duties to recommend reforms and keep indices; PAJA limits this to ministerial discretion to establish an advisory council, and non‑judicial review remains theoretical rather than implemented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The practical standard emerging from the article is that independent, sustained oversight (via an ARC or similar body) would improve administrative justice, but PAJA's discretionary approach means oversight may be weak unless the Minister or Parliament acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training and education of administrators
rubrics_metrics.description: Continued education and training of administrators about administrative law and PAJA is crucial; early 'train-the-trainer' workshops helped but awareness gaps (e.g., administrators not consulting empowering legislation) remain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article stresses that compliance with PAJA depends on practical training and attitude change among administrators; effective implementation requires sustained institutional training initiatives beyond mere promulgation of rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need to strengthen safeguards against corruption and maladministration
rubrics_metrics.description: Corruption undermines democratic ethos, rule of law and administrative justice; PAJA (and constitutional checks) should form part of an integrated response that strengthens safeguards against maladministration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article cites Glenister v President and commentary stressing that administrative law reforms must include measures to combat corruption; this is an evaluative standard for assessing whether administrative structures and PAJA implementation are adequate to protect rights and public trust.
